name: Algorithms
description: Complexity, sorting, searching, graph traversal, dynamic programming and the patterns behind most interview questions.

modules.name: Complexity & Analysis
modules.description: Big-O, amortised cost and how to reason about an algorithm before writing it.

cards.prompt: What do O, Ω and Θ actually describe?
cards.answer: O is an asymptotic upper bound, Ω a lower bound, Θ a tight bound. They describe growth as input size increases, ignoring constants and lower-order terms.
cards.explanation: 'Quicksort is O(n²)' is true but unhelpful; 'Θ(n log n) average, O(n²) worst' is the useful statement. Constants matter in practice: an O(n log n) algorithm with a huge constant loses to O(n²) at small n, which is why sorts switch to insertion sort under ~16 elements.

cards.prompt: Ordered from fastest to slowest growth: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ), O(___).
cards.answer: n!
cards.explanation: Factorial growth appears in brute-force permutation problems such as naive travelling salesman. Useful anchors: log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20; n log n on a million items is ~20 million operations (instant); n² on a million is 10¹² (hours).

cards.prompt: What is the time complexity of this function?
cards.code:
def f(items):
    seen = []
    for x in items:          # n
        if x not in seen:    # O(len(seen)) list scan
            seen.append(x)
    return seen
cards.answer: O(n²) — `x not in seen` is a linear scan performed n times. Using a set makes it O(n).
cards.explanation: The loop looks linear because the quadratic part hides inside an innocent-looking operator. Always ask what each library call costs: `in` on a list is O(n), on a set or dict it is O(1).

cards.prompt: Give three concrete examples of trading space for time.
cards.answer: Hash maps (memory for O(1) lookup), memoisation/caching (store results instead of recomputing), and precomputed indexes or lookup tables (build once, query cheaply).
cards.explanation: The reverse trade exists too: streaming algorithms and in-place sorts give up memory to fit constraints, and probabilistic structures such as Bloom filters or HyperLogLog trade exactness for tiny footprints.

modules.name: Sorting & Searching
modules.description: The sorts worth knowing, why libraries pick hybrids, and binary search done correctly.

cards.prompt: Quicksort vs merge sort
cards.answer: Quicksort is in-place and cache-friendly with O(n²) worst case; merge sort is stable with a guaranteed O(n log n) but needs O(n) extra space.

left.title: Quicksort
points: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst

right.title: Merge sort
points: Natural fit for linked lists and external sorting

cards.explanation: Real libraries use hybrids: introsort (quicksort + heapsort fallback + insertion sort for small ranges) in C++, and Timsort (merge sort exploiting existing runs) in Python and Java for objects — because stability matters when sorting records by multiple keys.

cards.prompt: What does a *stable* sort guarantee, and when do you need it?
cards.answer: Equal elements keep their relative input order. You need it for multi-key sorting: sort by name, then by department, and names stay ordered within each department.
cards.explanation: Without stability you must build a composite comparator instead of sorting in passes. Java's `Arrays.sort` is stable for objects (Timsort) but not for primitives (dual-pivot quicksort) — because primitives are indistinguishable when equal.

cards.prompt: This binary search has a bug that survived in production libraries for years. What is it?
cards.answer: `low + high` can overflow a 32-bit int for large arrays, producing a negative index. Use `low + (high - low) / 2` (or unsigned shift `>>> 1`).
cards.explanation: This exact bug lived in the JDK's `Arrays.binarySearch` for nine years. It is the standard reminder that a correct algorithm can still have an incorrect implementation — and that overflow is a real, not theoretical, failure mode.

resources.title: Google Research — Nearly all binary searches are broken

cards.prompt: Binary search on a sorted array: time and space?
cards.answer: O(log n) time, O(1) space iteratively.
cards.explanation: It requires random access and sorted data — which is why it works on arrays but not linked lists. If you must sort first, that O(n log n) dominates, so binary search only pays off across many queries on the same data.

cards.prompt: Find whether a sorted array contains two numbers summing to a target, in O(n) time and O(1) space.
cards.answer: Two pointers: one at each end. If the sum is too large move the right pointer left; too small, move the left pointer right; equal, done.
cards.explanation: Sortedness makes each move provably safe — a discarded pair could never have worked. The same pattern solves container-with-most-water, three-sum (after sorting), and palindrome checks. The hash-set alternative is O(n) time but O(n) space and works unsorted.

cards.prompt: When does the sliding-window pattern apply, and what does it replace?
cards.answer: When you need the best or a valid contiguous subarray/substring under a monotone constraint. It replaces the O(n·k) or O(n²) recomputation with incremental update as the window moves — O(n).
cards.explanation: Fixed-size windows (max sum of k elements) just add the entering and subtract the leaving element. Variable windows (longest substring without repeats, smallest subarray ≥ target) grow the right edge and shrink the left while the constraint is violated.

modules.name: Graphs, DP & Greedy
modules.description: Traversal, shortest paths, dynamic programming and knowing when greedy is actually correct.

cards.prompt: BFS vs DFS
cards.answer: BFS explores level by level with a queue and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS dives deep with a stack or recursion and suits ordering and connectivity problems.
cards.explanation: Both visit every vertex and edge once. Choose by what you need from the order: BFS if distance matters, DFS if structure does. On very deep graphs, DFS recursion can blow the stack — use an explicit stack.

cards.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary heap: complexity, and what assumption does it require?
cards.answer: O((V + E) log V). It requires non-negative edge weights.

complexity.time: O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap

cards.explanation: Negative edges break the greedy invariant that a settled node is final — use Bellman–Ford (O(VE), detects negative cycles) instead. A* is Dijkstra plus an admissible heuristic, which prunes the search without losing optimality.

cards.prompt: You must order build tasks so every dependency runs first, and report an error if that is impossible. What do you use?
cards.answer: Topological sort of the dependency DAG — Kahn's algorithm (repeatedly take nodes with in-degree 0) or DFS post-order reversed. If nodes remain with non-zero in-degree, there is a cycle.
cards.explanation: This is the algorithm behind make, npm, task schedulers, course prerequisites and spreadsheet recalculation. Kahn's version gives you cycle detection for free and parallelises naturally: every in-degree-0 node can run at once.

cards.prompt: What two properties must a problem have for dynamic programming to apply?
cards.answer: Optimal substructure (an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to subproblems) and overlapping subproblems (the same subproblems recur).
cards.explanation: Without overlap, plain divide and conquer is enough. Memoisation is top-down DP (recursion plus a cache); tabulation is bottom-up. Start by writing the recurrence and identifying the state — the code follows from those.

cards.prompt: What is the complexity before and after adding the cache?
cards.answer: Without the cache O(2ⁿ) time; with it O(n) time and O(n) space.
cards.explanation: The naive tree recomputes `fib(n-2)` exponentially often. Memoisation makes each state computed once, collapsing the tree to a linear chain — the clearest illustration of overlapping subproblems there is.

cards.prompt: When is a greedy algorithm provably correct, and give an example where it fails?
cards.answer: When the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure — as in interval scheduling by earliest finish time, Huffman coding, or Kruskal's MST. It fails on 0/1 knapsack, where taking the best ratio first can miss the optimum.
cards.explanation: Greedy is fast and simple but needs a proof — usually an exchange argument showing any optimal solution can be transformed into the greedy one without getting worse. Coin change is the classic trap: greedy works for {1,5,10,25} and fails for {1,3,4} on 6.

cards.prompt: What is backtracking, and what makes it tractable?
cards.answer: Systematic search that builds candidates incrementally and abandons a branch as soon as it cannot lead to a solution. Pruning is what keeps the exponential space manageable.
cards.explanation: N-queens, sudoku, subsets, permutations and constraint solvers are all backtracking. The template is: choose, explore, un-choose. Good pruning (constraint propagation, ordering by most-constrained variable) is worth far more than micro-optimising the loop.

modules.name: Analysis & Core Techniques
modules.description: Recurrences, amortised cost, lower bounds, prefix sums, monotonic stacks and binary search on the answer.

cards.prompt: What do the recurrences T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) and T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1) solve to?
cards.answer: Merge-sort shape: O(n log n). Binary-search shape: O(log n). Tree-traversal shape: O(n).

complexity.time: O(n log n), O(log n), O(n)

cards.explanation: The master theorem compares the work at the root, O(n^c), with the number of leaves, n^(log_b a). Leaves dominate → O(n^(log_b a)); balanced → multiply by log n; root dominates → O(n^c). Recognising these three shapes covers most divide-and-conquer analysis you will meet.

cards.prompt: Why can no comparison sort beat O(n log n), and how do counting and radix sort get around it?
cards.answer: A comparison sort must distinguish all n! orderings, and each comparison yields one bit, so it needs at least log₂(n!) ≈ n log n comparisons. Counting and radix sort do not compare elements — they index by key digits — so they run in O(n + k) or O(d·(n + k)) for bounded integer keys.
cards.explanation: Non-comparison sorts win when keys are small integers or fixed-width (ages, bytes, IPv4 addresses). The catch is memory proportional to the key range k and restriction to specific key types; for general objects, comparison sorting remains the tool.

cards.prompt: What does "amortised O(1)" mean, and how is it different from "average O(1)"?
cards.answer: Amortised cost is the worst-case total over any sequence of operations divided by the number of operations — occasional expensive steps are paid for by many cheap ones, guaranteed. Average-case is an expectation over random inputs and can be beaten by bad luck or an adversary.
cards.explanation: Dynamic-array append is amortised O(1): no sequence of n appends can cost more than O(n). Hash-table lookup is average O(1): adversarial keys can make every lookup O(n). The distinction matters for latency: amortised structures still have individual slow operations.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
from itertools import accumulate
a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
pre = [0, *accumulate(a)]
print(pre)
print(pre[4] - pre[1])
cards.explanation: A prefix-sum array stores `pre[i]` = the sum of the first i elements, built once in O(n). Any range sum `sum(a[l:r])` is then `pre[r] - pre[l]` in O(1): here `a[1:4]` is 1 + 4 + 1 = 6, computed as `pre[4] - pre[1]` = 9 − 3. The leading 0 removes the special case for ranges starting at index 0. The 2-D version answers rectangle sums in images and grids.

cards.prompt: For each day's temperature, find how many days until a warmer one — in O(n). Which technique?
cards.answer: A monotonic stack: keep indices of days with decreasing temperatures. For each new day, pop every index with a lower temperature and record the gap; then push the current index. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total is O(n).
cards.explanation: The same pattern solves "next greater element", largest rectangle in a histogram, stock span, and trapping rain water. The signal is "for each element, find the nearest element to one side that is bigger or smaller".

cards.prompt: Ship packages within D days using the smallest possible truck capacity. The check "can capacity C finish in D days?" is easy. How do you find the minimum C efficiently?
cards.answer: Binary search on the answer: feasibility is monotone in C (if C works, every larger C works), so search the range [max package, total weight] for the smallest feasible C — O(n log(sum)).
cards.explanation: Whenever the question is "the minimum X such that a monotone condition holds", search over X rather than over the input. It solves splitting arrays, Koko-eating-bananas style rate problems, and scheduling with deadlines. Write the check function first; the search is boilerplate.

cards.prompt: Finding the k largest of n items: cost of sorting, of a size-k min-heap, and of quickselect?
cards.answer: Sorting: O(n log n). A size-k min-heap: O(n log k), O(k) memory, and it works on streams. Quickselect: O(n) average (O(n²) worst), in place.

complexity.time: sort O(n log n); heap O(n log k); quickselect O(n) avg

cards.explanation: Heaps win on streams and when k is small; quickselect wins for a one-off on an in-memory array (`std::nth_element` in C++, `numpy.partition`). Python's `heapq.nlargest` switches strategies depending on k relative to n.

cards.prompt: Why does this crash on a list of 100,000 items, and what is the fix?
cards.answer: Each recursive call adds a stack frame, and Python's default recursion limit is about 1,000 (native stacks are only a few MB), so linear-depth recursion over big inputs overflows. Rewrite it as a loop or use an explicit stack; recursion is best when depth is logarithmic.
cards.explanation: Python and Java do not eliminate tail calls, so even a tail-recursive version still grows the stack. Recursion is natural for trees and divide-and-conquer, where depth is O(log n) if balanced — beware degenerate, list-shaped trees.

modules.name: Graphs & Strings II
modules.description: Minimum spanning trees, all-pairs and negative-weight shortest paths, A*, cycle detection and string matching.

cards.prompt: Kruskal vs Prim for a minimum spanning tree
cards.answer: Both are greedy and both are correct. Kruskal sorts all edges and adds the cheapest one that does not form a cycle (checked with union-find); Prim grows one tree from a start vertex, always adding the cheapest edge leaving it (using a priority queue).

left.title: Kruskal
points: Natural for sparse graphs and edge lists

right.title: Prim
points: Good for dense graphs (O(V²) array version)

cards.explanation: MSTs appear in network design, clustering (cut the heaviest MST edges) and as approximation building blocks. Correctness comes from the cut property: the lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST.

cards.prompt: Bellman–Ford vs Floyd–Warshall
cards.answer: Bellman–Ford computes single-source shortest paths with negative edges in O(VE) and detects negative cycles. Floyd–Warshall computes all-pairs shortest paths in O(V³) with a simple triple loop.

left.title: Bellman–Ford
points: Negative edges OK; reports negative cycles

cards.explanation: Choose by question: one source → Dijkstra (non-negative weights) or Bellman–Ford (negative weights); all pairs on a small dense graph → Floyd–Warshall; all pairs on a sparse graph → run Dijkstra from each vertex (Johnson's algorithm handles negatives).

cards.prompt: How does A* differ from Dijkstra, and what makes its heuristic admissible?
cards.answer: A* orders the frontier by f(n) = g(n) + h(n): the known cost so far plus a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost. The heuristic is admissible if it never overestimates the true remaining cost, which guarantees the path found is optimal.
cards.explanation: With h = 0, A* is Dijkstra. A good heuristic (straight-line or Manhattan distance on a grid) dramatically shrinks the search. An inadmissible heuristic can be faster but may return suboptimal paths — sometimes an acceptable trade in games.

resources.title: Red Blob Games — Introduction to A*

cards.prompt: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph versus an undirected one?
cards.answer: Directed: DFS with three colours (unvisited, on the current path, finished) — reaching a node that is still on the path means a back edge, hence a cycle. Or Kahn's algorithm leaving nodes unprocessed. Undirected: DFS finding a visited node that is not the parent, or union-find reporting two endpoints already connected.
cards.explanation: For linked lists, Floyd's tortoise-and-hare finds a cycle in O(1) space: move one pointer one step and another two steps — they meet if and only if there is a cycle.

resources.title: CP-Algorithms — Checking a graph for acyclicity

cards.prompt: Naive substring search is O(n·m). How do KMP and Rabin–Karp do better?
cards.answer: KMP precomputes, for each prefix of the pattern, the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix; on a mismatch it jumps using that table instead of re-scanning, giving O(n + m). Rabin–Karp compares rolling hashes of each window and checks characters only on a hash match — O(n + m) expected, and natural for searching many patterns.
cards.explanation: In practice, standard library `find` implementations use tuned algorithms (such as Two-Way or Boyer–Moore variants). Knowing KMP matters for the idea of a failure function, which reappears in Aho–Corasick for matching many patterns at once.

cards.prompt: Given meeting times, merge overlapping ones — and separately, find the minimum number of rooms needed. How?
cards.answer: Merge: sort by start, then extend the last merged interval while the next one starts before it ends — O(n log n). Rooms: sort start and end times separately (or sweep with a min-heap of end times) and track the maximum number of meetings open at once.
cards.explanation: Sorting first is the key move in nearly every interval problem. The sweep-line view — +1 at each start, −1 at each end, find the running maximum — generalises to calendar conflicts, bandwidth peaks and CPU scheduling.

modules.name: Dynamic Programming & Hardness
modules.description: Knapsack, edit distance, LIS, the DP recipe, and what NP-completeness means in practice.

cards.prompt: 0/1 knapsack with n items and capacity W: complexity of the classic DP, and why is it called pseudo-polynomial?
cards.answer: O(n·W) time and O(W) space with a 1-D table iterated from high to low capacity. It is pseudo-polynomial because the cost is polynomial in the numeric value of W but exponential in the number of bits used to write W down — each extra bit doubles the work.
cards.explanation: Knapsack is NP-complete, yet solvable quickly when W is small — that is the pseudo-polynomial loophole. Iterating capacity downwards in the 1-D version prevents an item from being used twice; iterating upwards gives the unbounded variant.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: Edit (Levenshtein) distance fills a table where `d[i][j]` is the cost to turn the first i characters of a into the first j of b, taking the minimum of delete, insert and substitute. kitten → sitting needs three edits: k→s, e→i, insert g. O(n·m) time; two rows suffice for space.

cards.prompt: Longest increasing subsequence: complexity of the straightforward DP, and of the patience-sorting method?
cards.answer: The DP over "LIS ending at i" is O(n²). Patience sorting keeps, for each length, the smallest possible tail value, and binary-searches where each element goes — O(n log n).

complexity.time: O(n²) DP; O(n log n) with binary search

cards.explanation: The tails array is always sorted, which is what makes binary search applicable; it does not itself hold a valid subsequence, but parent pointers recover one. LIS shows up in diff algorithms, box stacking and scheduling problems.

cards.prompt: What is a reliable recipe for solving a new dynamic programming problem?
cards.answer: Define the state (what parameters identify a subproblem), write the recurrence (how a state is built from smaller ones), identify base cases, choose an evaluation order (memoised recursion or a table filled in dependency order), then optimise space if only recent rows are needed.
cards.explanation: Most difficulty is in the state definition — "the best answer using the first i items with capacity w". If the recurrence needs information your state does not hold, add a dimension. Draw the table for a tiny example before writing code.

cards.prompt: What do P, NP, NP-complete and NP-hard mean — and what do you do when you meet an NP-complete problem at work?
cards.answer: P: solvable in polynomial time. NP: a proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time. NP-complete: in NP and every NP problem reduces to it (SAT, travelling salesman decision, graph colouring). NP-hard: at least as hard as NP-complete, not necessarily in NP. Whether P = NP is open.
cards.explanation: In practice: check whether your instances are small or specially structured, use approximation algorithms with guarantees, heuristics (greedy, local search, simulated annealing), or hand the problem to a SAT/ILP solver — modern solvers handle surprisingly large real instances.
